lead: Open source software is software whose source code is published under a licence that lets people study it, change it and share changed copies. The idea exists because closed software hides the code, so only the vendor can fix or extend it. In practice open source runs phones, web servers, data-centre tools and the Linux systems in this course. This chapter explains source code, licences, the benefits and the real costs.
prereq: You need: Chapter 1.1 for Unix and Linux history and Chapter 1.3 for kernel, shell and user space.

blocks.text: Source code is the human-readable form of a program: the C, Python or shell statements that a programmer writes. A compiler or interpreter turns it into machine instructions, often called binaries. When you buy closed software, you usually get binaries only. Open source software ships the source code as well, under a licence.

A licence is the legal document that says what you may do with the software. Copyright gives the author control by default: others may not copy, modify or redistribute without permission. An open-source licence gives those permissions on stated conditions. A copyleft licence, such as the GNU General Public License (GPL), requires anyone who distributes a modified version to use the same licence and provide source. The change stays open. A permissive licence, such as MIT or BSD, allows modification and redistribution, including inside closed products, provided copyright notices are kept. So open source is not one rule; the licence decides the duties.

Open source lowers lock-in: you can change vendor or hire another team because the code is available. Auditability is the power to inspect what the program does. A bank, hospital or election office can read the code or pay an auditor to check it, instead of trusting a vendor's promise. The licence usually carries no per-seat fee, so cost does not grow with every extra user or lab PC. Local customization is possible: a college can add a local language menu, and a firm can patch a bug that matters only to its workflow. Community support means bug reports, patches and documentation come from many users; a widespread problem is often fixed once and shared. Long-term use improves because the source survives even if the original vendor stops selling the product. These benefits are why Linux runs most web servers, Android phones and many government systems.

The benefits are real, but open source is not zero cost. Support may be bought from a company or handled by your own staff. Training takes time because tools differ from the old system. Migration has a one-time cost: converting files, testing printers and changing scripts. Staff time is a running cost. A fair comparison adds these items:
Total cost = licence fees + support + training + migration + staff time
blocks.where: licence fees is what you pay for the legal right to use the software; support is paid help; training is user and admin learning; migration is the one-time move from the old system; staff time is ongoing internal effort.

blocks.text: Here licence fees may be ₹0 for an open-source product, but the other terms are not zero. A proprietary product also has training and migration costs, so compare like with like. The licence still exists: it gives permissions and imposes conditions, such as keeping notices or sharing changes. 'Free' in free software means freedom to study, run, change and share, not a price tag. Freeware is different: it is free of charge but may hide its source and forbid modification.

figure.caption: Source is published, reviewed, built into packages and installed. The dashed path shows fixes returning from users to the source.

spec.aria: Source code goes to community review, then a built package, then users, whose fixes return to the source.

examples.question: A college needs an operating system for 40 lab PCs. A proprietary licence costs ₹8,000 per PC. A Linux distribution has ₹0 licence cost but ₹60,000 total support. Compute the proprietary licence cost, the open-source total, and the saving against the proprietary licence alone.
steps: Saving against the proprietary licence alone = ₹3,20,000 − ₹60,000 = ₹2,60,000.
examples.answer: The open-source route costs ₹60,000, so the saving against the proprietary licence alone is ₹2,60,000.
examples.check:
proprietary_per_pc = 8000
pcs = 40
proprietary_total = proprietary_per_pc * pcs
open_licence = 0
support = 60000
open_total = open_licence + support
saving = proprietary_total - open_total
print(proprietary_total)
print(open_total)
print(saving)

traps: Open source does not mean zero cost. Support, training, migration and staff time still cost money.
Open source is not 'no licence'. It has a licence that grants rights and often imposes duties, such as keeping notices or sharing changes.
'Free' in free software means freedom to study, run, change and share, not price. Freeware may cost nothing but can be closed.
Copyleft and permissive licences differ. GPL-style copyleft requires modified distributed versions to stay under the same licence; MIT and BSD allow closed products if notices are kept.
Publishing source is not enough. If the licence forbids modification or redistribution, the software is not open source in the usual sense.

quiz.a: Source code is the human-readable form of a program, such as C, Python or shell statements, before it is compiled or interpreted into machine instructions.

quiz.q: Name one copyleft licence and one permissive licence.
quiz.a: Copyleft: GNU General Public License (GPL). Permissive: MIT licence or BSD licence.

quiz.q: Why does a licence matter even when the source code is published?
quiz.a: Copyright gives the author control by default. A licence states what users may do: copy, modify, redistribute or combine with other code. Without a licence, publishing source does not grant those rights.

quiz.q: A lab has 25 PCs. A proprietary licence costs ₹6,000 per PC. An open-source setup has ₹0 licence cost and ₹45,000 total support. Compute the saving against the proprietary licence alone.
Give two reasons a company may still pay for support on open source.
quiz.a: It may need a guaranteed response time for critical systems, and its own staff may lack deep knowledge of the software. Paid support can also provide security patches, testing and help during migration.

quiz.q: Why can copyleft increase long-term availability but limit mixing with closed code?
quiz.a: Copyleft requires distributed modified versions to stay under the same licence and provide source, so improvements remain available to later users. That same requirement can stop a firm from putting the code into a closed product without releasing its changes, so legal review is needed.

Open source means the source code is available under a licence that allows study, modification and redistribution. Freeware means the software costs nothing to use; its source may be hidden and modification may be forbidden.

beyond: Not for exam. In industry, open-source use is tracked through licence inventories and software bills of materials, because a single dependency can carry duties. Security teams watch upstream projects for fixes and review who may change the code. Governments and universities often publish tools under permissive licences to encourage reuse. Researchers study how shared maintenance affects reliability and long-term cost. Useful search terms: copyleft, permissive licence, software bill of materials, open-source program office.
